title: Doppler Effect: Moving Sound Source and Observed Frequency Shift
topic: Wave Physics - Acoustics and Relative Motion
pedagogical_goal: Visualize and quantify how the motion of a sound source relative to a stationary observer compresses or stretches sound waves, leading to observable increases (blueshift) or decreases (redshift) in perceived frequency, while reinforcing that wave speed in the medium remains constant.

fundamental_laws: Observed frequency: f' = f * (v / (v ∓ vs)), where upper sign (-) is for source approaching observer, lower sign (+) for receding.
Wavelength shift: λ' = λ * (v ∓ vs) / v, with same sign convention.
Wave speed invariance: v = fλ = f'λ' (constant in medium).

components.description: A trapezoidal sound source (speaker-like) emitting concentric circular wavefronts. Positioned at x=200, y=240. When source_velocity > 0 (moving right/toward observer), wavefronts are compressed on the right (observer side) and expanded on the left. Path: M 180 220 l 40 0 l 20 20 l -40 0 z. Wavefronts are dashed circles with radius increasing over time, spaced according to wavelength_observed on right and wavelength_original on left.

A filled circle representing the observer's ear at x=800, y=240, radius 12, fill accent color. Receives wavefronts; the frequency of arrival is visualized by a pulsating glow (gsap) matching observed_frequency.

Series of 8 concentric semicircular arcs (only right half shown for clarity) emanating from the sound source. Each arc is a path segment of a circle with radii: n * wavelength_observed (if source moving toward observer) or n * wavelength_original (if moving away). Arcs are stroked with primary color, stroke-width 2, dash-array simulating compression/expansion. Dynamically regenerated based on source_velocity and source_frequency.

A double-headed arrow above the wavefronts showing wavelength. Left side: original wavelength (λ0). Right side: observed wavelength (λ'). Length scales with calculated values. Label shows numeric values. Updates in real-time.

A sinusoidal wave (y = A * sin(2π * f' * t)) propagating from source to observer, representing pressure variation. Amplitude 20px, frequency tied to observed_frequency. Drawn as a thin stroke path with glow effect. Demonstrates how more wave cycles fit in same distance when source approaches.

lifecycle_rules: Use React useRef for SVG/DOM node references (sound_source, wavefronts, observer_glow, frequency_waves)
Use gsap.context() inside useEffect for cleanup
Animate wavefront expansion using gsap.to() on a custom 'waveRadius' variable (0 to 400) with repeat: -1, ease: 'none'
Pulse observer glow with gsap.to() scaling fill opacity and filter: drop-shadow, duration = 1 / observed_frequency, repeat: -1, yoyo: true
Animate frequency_waves path drawing using stroke-dashoffset with gsap.to() over duration of one period
Smoothly tween reactive state changes (source_velocity, source_frequency) using gsap.to(vars, {duration: 0.5})

pedagogical_callouts.title: Stationary Source: Symmetric Wavefronts
pedagogical_callouts.text: When the sound source is stationary (vs = 0), wavefronts are evenly spaced circles. The observer detects the same frequency as the source. Wavelength and frequency obey v = fλ.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Source Moving Toward Observer: Wavefront Compression
pedagogical_callouts.text: As the source moves toward the observer, each successive wavefront is emitted from a position closer to the observer. This compresses the wavelength in front of the source (increasing observed frequency) and stretches it behind (decreasing frequency behind).

pedagogical_callouts.title: Observer Perspective: Higher Pitch Detected
pedagogical_callouts.text: The stationary observer encounters wavefronts more frequently due to the reduced spacing (λ' < λ). This results in a higher perceived pitch (blueshift). The wave speed in the medium remains unchanged.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Source Moving Away: Wavefront Stretch and Redshift
pedagogical_callouts.text: When the source recedes, wavefronts are stretched behind it (λ' > λ), leading to fewer wavefronts reaching the observer per second—a lower perceived pitch (redshift). The Doppler formula adjusts sign accordingly.
